prompt: An amplitude attack lasts only about one or two control-update intervals. The engine holds each control value for an entire block. Why is that a problem, and what should change?

options.text: The attack will become a finely sampled curve simply because the audio sample rate is high
options.explanation: The audio samples all reuse the same held value within each block; the envelope itself remains coarse.

options.text: The attack becomes a few large steps; evaluate it per sample or use suitable within-block interpolation
options.explanation: Correct. The update rate must resolve the fast control event, not just the audio carrier.

options.text: Reduce the update rate further to smooth the attack
options.explanation: Fewer updates give fewer, larger held steps.

options.text: Change the envelope’s name from control to audio
options.explanation: A label does not alter the actual update behaviour.

workedExample: Inspect how many distinct envelope values the short attack actually receives. Holding only one or two updates creates large jumps even though thousands of audio samples are processed each second. Move fast envelope work into the sample loop or design interpolation that represents the intended transition.

link.title: Sinusoidal FM and PM — Julius O. Smith

prompt: Which statements about control-rate and audio-rate modulation are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Interpolating control values linearly across each block removes most of the block-rate staircase
options.explanation: Correct. The parameter then changes every sample, just with a piecewise-linear shape.

options.text: Control rate is always fine for amplitude envelopes because envelopes are 'slow'
options.explanation: Fast attacks can span only a few control updates at typical block sizes, producing coarse steps that may click depending on signal and playback conditions.

options.text: A 5 Hz LFO updated at a 1.5 kHz control rate gets about 300 updates per cycle, which is ample
options.explanation: Correct. 1500 / 5 = 300 points per cycle, as in the LFO unit's code.

options.text: Lowering the control rate always makes modulation sound smoother
options.explanation: Fewer updates mean bigger steps: rougher, not smoother.

options.text: Audible-frequency pitch modulation is FM and belongs in this voice’s per-sample path
options.explanation: Correct. The modulation needs sufficient update bandwidth. The low control rates in these examples cannot represent an arbitrary audible-frequency modulator; use the per-sample path, with oversampling or other alias-reduction measures when needed.

workedExample:
Rule of thumb: the update rate must be high relative to how fast the modulation changes.

| Signal | Typical home |
|---|---|
| Slow LFO | control rate |
| Mod wheel | control + smooth |
| Amp env | per sample |
| Audible-frequency FM | per sample |

Interpolating within each block is the standard cheap compromise.
